a: David came to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest
t: Nob, the town of the priests
p: After Shiloh fell, the priests of Eli's family settled at Nob, within sight of Jerusalem.
b: Nob stood on a hill just north or east of Jerusalem; Isaiah pictures an invader at Nob shaking his fist at Mount Zion (Isaiah 10:32). After the Philistines took the ark and Shiloh faded (chapter 4), the priests of Eli's line seem to have moved here, so that 22:19 can call Nob "the priests' town." Ahimelech son of Ahitub is a great-grandson of Eli. He may be the same man as Ahijah son of Ahitub, who carried the ephod for Saul (14:3), or his brother. David comes alone, and the priest trembles, as the elders of Bethlehem trembled when Samuel arrived (16:4): a visit from a powerful man could mean trouble.

a: The king gave me a job to do
p: David invents a secret mission from Saul. The narrator does not comment, but the cost comes in chapter 22.
b: David is not on the king's business; he is running from the king. The story reports the lie without a word of judgment, and readers have weighed it in different ways. Many Jewish and Christian interpreters excuse it as a lie told to save a life, like the midwives' answer to Pharaoh (Exodus 1:19) or Rahab's (Joshua 2:4–6). Others point out that the lie protects David but kills the priests, who could not defend themselves because they did not know the truth (22:15). David himself later says, "I have caused the loss of every life in your father's house" (22:22). Literary readers (the L lens) note that the narrator often lets events judge a character instead of stating a verdict.

a: such-and-such a spot
p: The Hebrew peloni almoni is a way of not naming something, like English "so-and-so."
b: Hebrew peloni almoni is used when a speaker will not or need not give a name. Boaz uses it for the nearer relative whose name the book of Ruth never gives (Ruth 4:1), and the king of Aram uses it for a camp site he keeps secret (2 Kings 6:8). Here it fits David's story of a secret mission: he will not even tell the priest where his men are. Whether those young men exist at all is left unclear; David arrives alone (21:1).
orig: פְּלֹנִי אַלְמוֹנִי (peloni almoni), "a certain, unnamed one"

a: only holy bread
t: The holy bread and the rule about women
p: The Presence Bread was for priests, eaten in a holy place. Ahimelech adds a rule of purity for David's men.
b: Twelve loaves were set on a gold table in the sanctuary every Sabbath, and the old loaves went to the priests to be eaten in a holy place (Leviticus 24:5–9). Ahimelech is willing to bend that rule for hungry men, but only if they are ritually clean. Sexual relations made a person unclean until evening (Leviticus 15:18), and Israelites kept away from women before meeting God at Sinai (Exodus 19:15) and in a war camp (Deuteronomy 23:9–14). Uriah's refusal to sleep with his wife while the army was in the field shows the same custom (2 Samuel 11:11).

a: Even on an ordinary trip the young men keep their gear holy
p: David's answer is one of the most difficult sentences in the chapter. Its key word can mean gear, weapons or bodies.
b: The Hebrew kelim means "vessels" or "things": tools, bags, weapons. Some interpreters take it here as a polite word for the men's bodies (compare 1 Thessalonians 4:4, where Paul's "vessel" may mean the same). The last clause is also unclear. The KJV takes the subject to be the bread: "the bread is in a manner common." Most modern readers take David to mean that his men are kept holy even on a normal march, so they are all the more holy on this one. The Plain English keeps "gear" and the general sense: David assures the priest that his men are clean.
orig: כְּלֵי־הַנְּעָרִים קֹדֶשׁ (keley hanne'arim qodesh), "the young men's vessels are holy"

a: the Presence Bread
p: Jesus used this story to answer critics of his disciples, and Mark's version raises a famous puzzle.
b: When Pharisees objected that Jesus' disciples picked grain on the Sabbath, Jesus asked whether they had read what David did when he and his men were hungry (Mark 2:25–26; Matthew 12:3–4; Luke 6:3–4). Human need could outweigh a rule about holy food. The rabbis made a similar point: the Talmud says David was allowed the bread because his life was in danger, and it discusses whether the day was a Sabbath (Menachot 95b). Mark dates the event "while Abiathar was high priest," but here the priest is Ahimelech, Abiathar's father. Some take Mark to mean "in the passage about Abiathar"; others note that the names are confused elsewhere too (2 Samuel 8:17); many critical scholars call it a slip.
r: Mark 2:23–28; Matthew 12:1–8; Luke 6:1–5; 2 Samuel 8:17; 1 Chronicles 18:16; Exodus 25:30

a: held at the sanctuary before the LORD
p: Doeg was "held back" at the sanctuary. The text does not say why.
b: The Hebrew ne'tsar means "restrained" or "kept in." Doeg may have been keeping a vow, waiting to be declared clean, or seeking refuge. Whatever the reason, the narrator plants him here as a silent witness. He will speak at the worst possible moment (22:9). David knows at once that his presence is dangerous (22:22).

a: He was named Doeg
p: The rabbis turned Doeg into a learned man ruined by an evil tongue, one of four commoners with no share in the world to come.
b: The Mishnah names Doeg with Balaam, Ahithophel and Gehazi as men who have no share in the world to come (Sanhedrin 10:2). The Talmud makes him a great scholar of the law whose learning did not reach his heart, and it treats his report to Saul as the classic case of lashon hara, harmful speech: it killed the one who spoke, the one who listened and the one spoken about (Arakhin 15b). Psalm 52, which its heading ties to Doeg, attacks a "mighty man" who loves evil and a tongue "like a sharpened razor."

a: The sword of Goliath the Philistine
p: The sword David once took from Goliath had been laid up at the sanctuary as a trophy.
b: After killing Goliath with his own sword, David took the giant's weapons (17:51, 54). Here the sword is kept at Nob, wrapped in a cloak behind the ephod, as a holy trophy, the way the Philistines later put Saul's armor in their goddess's temple (31:10). It is a sharp irony that David carries Goliath's sword into Goliath's hometown of Gath (21:10). Critical scholars note that 17:54 says David took Goliath's head to Jerusalem and his weapons to his tent, and see different traditions; others think the sword was given to the sanctuary later.

a: behind the ephod
p: An ephod could be a linen apron worn by priests, or something larger that stood or hung in a shrine.
b: The ephod appears in several forms. The priests of Nob "wore a linen ephod" (22:18), as the boy Samuel did (2:18). The high priest's ephod held the Urim and Thummim, used to ask God yes-or-no questions (Exodus 28:6–30). Gideon's ephod of gold stood in his town and became an idol (Judges 8:27). Here a sword can be kept "behind" it, so it seems to be an object hanging or standing in the sanctuary. This is the ephod Abiathar will carry to David (23:6).

a: He came to Achish king of Gath
p: Gath, Goliath's city, was the largest Philistine city in David's time. Its king bears a non-Semitic name.
b: Gath is Tell es-Safi, on the edge of the Shephelah; excavations led by Aren Maeir show it was a large city in the 900s BC, until the Arameans destroyed it about 830 BC (2 Kings 12:17). The name Achish appears again in a royal inscription found at Ekron, dated to the 600s BC, where a later king of Ekron is called 'kysh, written Ikausu in Assyrian records. Some scholars link the name to the Greek Achaios, "Achaean," which fits the Aegean origin of the Philistines. Fleeing to Saul's enemies is a desperate move, and David arrives carrying the sword of Gath's own champion.

a: king of the land
p: The Philistines already call David a king. Saul feared exactly this.
b: Achish's servants may mean only that David is a great local chief. But the reader knows that Samuel has anointed him (16:13), that Jonathan expects him to be king (20:15; 23:17), and that Saul fears it (18:8; 20:31). Foreigners speak the truth before Israel's own people say it aloud. Readers in the X lens have compared the Magi's question, "Where is the newborn king of the Jews?"

a: 'Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his tens of thousands'
p: The victory song first sung in 18:7 follows David everywhere. It is quoted three times in 1 Samuel.
b: The song appears first after Goliath's death (18:7), then here, and again when the Philistine commanders refuse to fight beside David (29:5). In Hebrew poetry "thousands" and "tens of thousands" are a common pair, used for one idea said twice (Deuteronomy 32:30; Psalm 91:7; Micah 6:7), so the women may not have meant to rank David above Saul. Saul heard it as a ranking (18:8), and so do the Philistines. The song that made David famous now puts his life at risk.

a: So in front of them he hid his good sense
p: Two psalm headings tie psalms to this scene, and one names the king as Abimelech.
b: The heading of Psalm 34 reads: "Of David, when he changed his behavior in front of Abimelech, who drove him out, and he went away" (Psalm 34:0). "Changed his behavior" is the same rare phrase as this verse, shinnah et ta'mo, literally "changed his sense." The heading of Psalm 56 places that psalm "when the Philistines seized him in Gath" (Psalm 56:0). Psalm 34 calls Achish Abimelech, the name of the Philistine king of Gerar in Genesis. Some think Abimelech was a royal title, as Pharaoh was in Egypt; others think the heading was written from memory. Scholars debate how old these headings are (see the topic page).
r: Psalm 34:0; Psalm 34:1–22; Psalm 56:0; Psalm 56:1–13; Genesis 20:2; Genesis 26:1

a: in their grip he played the madman
p: A midrash tells of David asking why God created madness, and learning the answer in Gath.
b: The Midrash on Psalms (on Psalm 34) tells that David once asked God what use there was in madness. In Gath he found out: pretending to be mad saved his life. The same midrash adds that Achish's own wife and daughter were mad, which explains his complaint, "Do I lack crazy people?" (21:15). Ancient peoples often treated the insane with a mix of pity, fear and contempt; a madman was not worth killing. David's act also explains Psalm 34:4, "he rescued me from everything I feared."

a: the cave of Adullam
p: Adullam lay in the low hills of Judah, about 13 miles west-southwest of Bethlehem.
b: Adullam was an old Canaanite town in the Shephelah (Joshua 12:15; 15:35), where Judah once had a friend named Hirah (Genesis 38:1). The hills there are full of caves. David's band later used "the stronghold" and the cave of Adullam as a base in the war with the Philistines (2 Samuel 23:13–17). The headings of Psalm 57 and Psalm 142 set those psalms "in the cave"; tradition has linked them with Adullam or with En-gedi (24:3). His family joins him because Saul might take revenge on them.
r: Joshua 15:35; Genesis 38:1; 2 Samuel 23:13–17; 1 Chronicles 11:15; Psalm 57:0; Psalm 142:0

a: Every man in a tight spot, every man with a lender after him, and every man with a bitter heart
p: Debtors and the bitter gather to David. Ancient Near Eastern texts know such bands of uprooted men.
b: Before the monarchy, Jephthah gathered "empty men" around him (Judges 11:3), and Abimelech hired some (Judges 9:4). Letters from Canaan in the 1300s BC (the Amarna letters) complain of the 'apiru, uprooted people who lived as raiders or hired soldiers. Many historians see David's band in that light: men who had lost land through debt and lived outside the law. Christian preachers have often seen a picture of Christ, who gathers the burdened and gives them a new captain (Matthew 11:28). Both readings note that this ragged troop becomes the core of David's army, his "mighty men" (2 Samuel 23:8–39).

a: David moved on from there to Mizpah of Moab
p: David's great-grandmother was Ruth the Moabite, which may explain why he trusted the king of Moab.
b: The book of Ruth ends with Ruth's son Obed, "the father of Jesse, the father of David" (Ruth 4:17). So David had family ties to Moab, and Moab, an enemy of Saul (14:47), had reason to welcome him. The friendship did not last. As king, David defeated Moab and killed two thirds of its captured soldiers (2 Samuel 8:2). A rabbinic tradition explains the change: the king of Moab murdered David's parents (Numbers Rabbah 14:1). The Bible itself does not say what happened to them.

a: Gad the prophet
p: Gad appears here for the first time. He will be David's prophet for the rest of his life.
b: Gad later brings David the LORD's choice of punishment after the census and tells him to build an altar on Araunah's threshing floor, the future temple site (2 Samuel 24:11–19). Chronicles calls him "David's seer," says he helped arrange the temple music, and names "the records of Gad the seer" as a source for David's reign (1 Chronicles 29:29; 2 Chronicles 29:25). His first word sends David back into Judah, the land he will rule, rather than letting him sit safe abroad.

a: beneath the tamarisk at the high place
p: Saul holds court under a tree with his spear in his hand. He will be buried under a tamarisk too.
b: Saul's spear is never far from his hand in these chapters (18:10; 19:9; 20:33; 26:7). Here he sits like a judge of old under a tree, as Deborah did (Judges 4:5) and as Saul himself did at Gibeah (14:2). The Hebrew ba-ramah could mean "on the height" or "at Ramah," but Ramah was Samuel's town, not Saul's. The story will end with Saul's bones buried "beneath the tamarisk in Jabesh" (31:13). Abraham planted a tamarisk at Beersheba and called on the LORD there (Genesis 21:33); Saul's tree is a seat of suspicion.

a: Is the son of Jesse going to hand out fields and vineyards to every one of you?
p: Saul appeals to tribal loyalty and land grants, the very thing Samuel warned a king would do.
b: Saul's servants are from his own tribe, Benjamin. He reminds them that a king from Judah would reward his own people instead. Samuel had warned that a king would take the people's best fields and vineyards and give them to his servants (8:14). Saul's speech shows that warning come true: his court runs on gifts and favors. He also calls David only "the son of Jesse," refusing to say his name (20:27; 22:8–9). Literary readers note how the scene shows a king cut off from trust, who sees plots everywhere.

a: nobody whispered it in my ear
p: The Hebrew idiom for telling someone a secret is "to uncover his ear." Saul uses it twice here and once more in 22:17.
b: The phrase galah ozen pictures lifting back someone's hair or headcloth to speak into the ear. It is used when God reveals something to Samuel (9:15) and when Jonathan says his father tells him everything (20:2). Saul repeats it bitterly: no one uncovers his ear. The repetition shows a man who feels shut out of his own kingdom.
orig: גֹּלֶה אֶת־אָזְנִי (goleh et ozni), "uncovers my ear"

a: Doeg the Edomite spoke up
p: The heading of Psalm 52 ties that psalm to Doeg's report.
b: The heading reads: "For the music director. A maskil of David, when Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul, 'David has gone to Ahimelech's house'" (Psalm 52:0). The psalm attacks a "mighty man" who boasts in evil and loves every word that devours, and it ends with the singer as "a leafy olive tree in God's house" (Psalm 52:8). The contrast fits the story: Doeg was found "before the LORD" at the sanctuary (21:7), but he destroyed it; the faithful one will flourish in God's house.

a: Ahimelech consulted the LORD for him
p: Chapter 21 does not say that Ahimelech asked God for David. Doeg adds it, and the priest does not deny it.
b: Doeg tells the truth about the bread and the sword, but chapter 21 says nothing about an inquiry of the LORD. Some readers think Doeg added it to make the charge worse, since asking God for guidance on someone's behalf was a royal privilege. Others note that Ahimelech's answer, "Is today the first day I have consulted God for him?" (22:15), seems to admit it. If so, the narrator held the detail back until the trial, a common technique in Hebrew storytelling.

a: Among all your servants, who can be trusted like David?
p: Ahimelech's defense uses the word "faithful," which the book attaches to priests, prophets and David's future house.
b: The Hebrew ne'eman, "faithful, trustworthy, firm," is a key word in Samuel. God promised to raise up "a faithful priest" and build him "a sure house" in place of Eli's (2:35). Samuel was recognized as "trustworthy" as a prophet (3:20). Abigail will promise David "a house that stands firm" (25:28), and Nathan will say the same (2 Samuel 7:16). Ahimelech, a priest of Eli's doomed house, speaks the word over David, and dies for it. His defense is honest and brave; it simply does not matter to Saul.

a: The king told the runners who stood around him
p: Saul's own guards will not kill the priests. It is one of the Bible's first stories of soldiers refusing an order.
b: "Runners" were the king's foot guards, who ran beside his chariot (8:11; 2 Samuel 15:1) and kept his palace (1 Kings 14:27–28; 2 Kings 11:4–6). Their refusal is a quiet act of conscience, like the troops who would not let Saul put Jonathan to death (14:45), and like the Hebrew midwives who would not kill Israel's baby boys (Exodus 1:17). Only Doeg, a foreigner with no tie to Israel's priests, will do it. Many readers have pointed to this scene in debates over whether a soldier must obey an order that breaks God's law.

a: men who wore a linen ephod
p: The slaughter at Nob fulfills, in part, the prophecy against the house of Eli.
b: A man of God had warned Eli that his family would be cut down, that no one in it would reach old age, and that one would be left to grieve (2:31–33); the LORD repeated the warning to young Samuel (3:11–14). Ahimelech is Eli's great-grandson (14:3). The priests in their linen ephods die, and one son, Abiathar, escapes (22:20). The prophecy closes when Solomon removes Abiathar from the priesthood, so that the word the LORD spoke at Shiloh about Eli's house came true (1 Kings 2:27). The text does not say that the priests of Nob deserved death; it shows an old word coming true through a wicked king.

a: man and woman, child and nursing baby, ox, donkey and sheep
t: The ban carried out on the wrong people
p: Saul does to an Israelite town of priests exactly what he refused to do to Amalek.
b: When Samuel sent Saul against Amalek, the order used this same list: "man and woman, child and nursing baby, ox and sheep, camel and donkey" (15:3). Saul spared the king and the best animals (15:9) and lost his kingdom for it. Now he wipes out Nob, the priests' own town, down to the animals. The echo is deliberate: the king who would not carry out the LORD's judgment on Israel's enemy carries out his own vengeance on the LORD's priests. The law imposed the ban on an Israelite town only if it turned to other gods (Deuteronomy 13:12–16).

a: Abiathar was his name
p: The only survivor of Nob becomes David's priest and carries the ephod through his reign.
b: From now on David has a priest and an ephod, and he can ask God for guidance (23:6, 9; 30:7), while Saul cannot get an answer (28:6). Abiathar serves David to the end, sharing the high priesthood with Zadok (2 Samuel 15:24–29), but he backs Adonijah against Solomon and is sent home to Anathoth (1 Kings 2:26–27). The prophet Jeremiah came from a priestly family at Anathoth (Jeremiah 1:1), and many have guessed he was Abiathar's descendant.

a: I knew it on that day
p: David admits that he saw the danger at Nob. It is the first time in the book he confesses a fault.
b: David noticed Doeg at Nob and still told his story and took the bread and sword. Now he says it plainly. Commentators across traditions honor the confession: David does not blame Saul alone. Some also see a pattern: David's choices often cost other people their lives (Uriah in 2 Samuel 11; the plague in 2 Samuel 24), and his response, at his best, is to own it. His promise to Abiathar, "With me you are under guard," begins to make up for it.

a: They are stripping the threshing floors bare
p: The Philistines strike Keilah when the grain is on the threshing floors, the whole year's food in one place.
b: Keilah (Khirbet Qila) was a walled town in the Shephelah of Judah, about 3 miles south of Adullam (Joshua 15:44). At harvest the grain lay out in the open on threshing floors, so raiders came then, as the Midianites did in Gideon's day (Judges 6:3–4, 11). Losing the threshing floor meant a year of hunger. Saul, the king, does nothing; the outlaw David rescues a town of Judah.

a: So David asked the LORD
t: The man who asks and the man named "Asked"
p: The verb "ask" (sha'al) sounds like Saul's name. David asks and is answered; Saul is not.
b: To "ask the LORD" (sha'al ba-YHWH) means to seek a decision through the priest's ephod or lot. The wordplay on Saul's name, Sha'ul, "asked for," is explained at 1:28 and 12:13. What is new in these chapters is the contrast: David asks again and again and gets clear answers (23:2, 4, 10–12; 30:8). Saul asks and gets silence (28:6), and finally asks a dead man, who answers, "Then why ask me?" (28:16). Robert Polzin and Robert Alter both trace this thread to its end at Endor.
orig: וַיִּשְׁאַל דָּוִד בַּיהוָה (vayyish'al David ba-YHWH), "David asked of the LORD"

a: an ephod came down with him, in his hand
p: The answers in this chapter are short, like the result of drawing lots: "He is coming down." "They will give you up."
b: How the Urim and Thummim worked is explained at 14:41. This chapter shows the method in use. David breaks his questions into simple pieces (23:10–12), and the answers are a single word in Hebrew: yered, "he will come down," yasgiru, "they will hand over." The verse is placed here to explain where David's ephod came from: Abiathar carried it out of Nob (22:20). The Hebrew word order is awkward, and the Greek reads it more smoothly, but the sense is the same.

a: God has given him up into my hand
p: Saul claims God's help, but the verb he uses is unusual. The Greek has "sold."
b: The Hebrew nikkar usually means "treat as a stranger" or "disown." Saul seems to mean that God has given David up. The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament made before Jesus, reads "has sold him," which suggests a Hebrew makar, the usual word for God selling someone into an enemy's power (Judges 4:9). Either way, Saul is sure God is on his side, though the narrator says the opposite in 23:14.

a: Will the leading men of Keilah give me up to him?
t: God's answer about what would have happened
p: God tells David what Saul and Keilah will do, and then it does not happen. Theologians have argued over this for centuries.
b: David learns that Saul will come and Keilah will hand him over. He leaves, so neither thing happens (23:13). Theologians cite this passage, with Matthew 11:21–23, as evidence that God knows what free people would do in situations that never arise. The Spanish Jesuit Luis de Molina (1588) built his idea of "middle knowledge" partly on it. Reformed theologians answer that God simply knows all possibilities as part of his knowledge. Open theists read it as God describing likely outcomes. Jewish commentators such as Radak read the answer as conditional: "if you stay." All agree that the warning was meant to be acted on.

a: the leading men of Keilah
p: The Hebrew ba'alim here means the town's citizens or landowners, the men who decide its policy.
b: Ba'alei Qe'ilah, "the lords of Keilah," are the town's full citizens, like "the lords of Shechem" who made Abimelech king (Judges 9:2–6) or "the lords of Jericho" (Joshua 24:11). David has just saved their harvest, but they will not risk Saul's anger for him. After Nob, no town could be blamed for fearing Saul.

a: yet God never put him into Saul's hands
p: "Hand" is the key word of these chapters. Everyone talks about who will be put into whose hand.
b: Saul says God has given David "into my hand" (23:7); the narrator says God never did (23:14). Jonathan says Saul's hand will not find David (23:17). David's men say God has put Saul into David's hand (24:4), and David refuses to stretch out his hand against him (24:6, 10; 26:9, 11, 23). Abigail stops David from saving himself "by his own hand" (25:26, 33). The question running through the story is whether David will take the kingdom by his own hand or receive it from God's.

a: when he became aware
p: The same Hebrew letters can be read "David saw" or "David was afraid."
b: The Masoretic vowels read vayyar', "he saw." Without vowels the word could also be vayyira', "he was afraid," and several modern translations read it so. Jonathan's first words in 23:17, "Have no fear," fit the second reading. The Plain English follows the vowels but keeps the sense of sudden realization.
orig: וַיַּרְא (vayyar'), "and he saw"; possibly וַיִּרָא (vayyira'), "and he feared"

a: He made David's hand strong in God
p: Jonathan's last visit strengthens David's hand. Later, alone, David will strengthen himself in the LORD.
b: "To strengthen someone's hands" means to encourage him (Judges 9:24; 2 Samuel 2:7; Nehemiah 2:18). Jonathan does it "in God," by pointing David to God's promise. This is the last time the two friends meet. At his lowest point, with no friend left, David will do the same thing for himself: "David made himself strong in the LORD his God" (30:6). Jonathan's gift becomes David's habit.

a: and I will be next to you, second in rank
p: The crown prince gives up his claim to the throne. He will not live to stand beside David.
b: Jonathan, the king's eldest son, knows David will be king and accepts it. He hopes only to serve at David's side. He will die with his father at Gilboa (31:2) before that can happen. Jewish tradition holds up the two friends as the model of love that does not depend on gain: "Love that depends on nothing never fails. Which is that? The love of David and Jonathan" (Mishnah Avot 5:16). Christian readers have compared John the Baptist: "He must keep growing, and I must keep getting smaller" (John 3:30).

a: Then men of Ziph went up to Saul at Gibeah
p: Psalm 54's heading ties it to the Ziphites' betrayal. The story will happen twice.
b: The heading reads: "For the music director. With stringed instruments. A maskil of David, when the Ziphites came and said to Saul, 'David is hiding among us, isn't he?'" (Psalm 54:0). The psalm complains that "outsiders have stood up against me" (Psalm 54:3), though the Ziphites were people of Judah, David's own tribe (Joshua 15:24, 55). Ziph (Tell Zif) lay about 4 miles southeast of Hebron, on the edge of the wilderness. The Ziphites betray David again in 26:1.

a: among all the thousands of Judah
p: A "thousand" (elef) was also a clan or military unit. Micah uses the same phrase about Bethlehem.
b: The Hebrew elef means "thousand," but it also names a clan, the unit that sent a company to war (Judges 6:15, where Gideon's "clan" is literally his "thousand"). Saul vows to hunt David through every clan of Judah. Micah later speaks to Bethlehem, "too small to be among the thousands of Judah," from which a ruler of Israel will come (Micah 5:2). The phrase links Saul's manhunt to the clan he is hunting: David's.

a: Just then a messenger reached Saul
p: At the last moment a Philistine raid pulls Saul away. Is this chance or God's hand?
b: Saul's men are circling the mountain and closing in when the news arrives. The narrator does not say God sent the Philistines, but the timing and the earlier verdict ("God never put him into Saul's hands," 23:14) invite readers to see providence at work, as in the book of Esther, where God is never named. Historians note that a Philistine raid on Judah's lowlands while Saul's army was deep in the wilderness is exactly what an alert enemy would do. Both readings can be true at once.

a: Sela-hammahlekoth
p: The name can mean "Rock of Divisions" or "Rock of Slipping Away." Both fit.
b: Sela' is "rock" or "cliff"; machleqot comes from chalaq, which can mean "divide" or "be smooth, slippery." So the place could be "the Rock of Parting," where Saul and David went separate ways, or "the Rock of Escape," where David slipped through Saul's fingers. Hebrew place names often keep the memory of an event this way (Genesis 28:19; Judges 15:17–19).

a: the hideouts at En-gedi
p: En-gedi is a spring-fed oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea, full of caves and wild goats.
b: En-gedi ("spring of the young goat") pours water down a cliff into a green gorge above the Dead Sea, in the middle of a bare desert. The limestone hills around it are full of caves, and Nubian ibex still climb there. The Song of Songs praises its vineyards (Song of Songs 1:14), and Ezekiel sees fishermen there when the sea is healed (Ezekiel 47:10). In Hebrew Bibles this verse is numbered 24:1, so the verse numbers in chapter 24 run one higher in Hebrew than in English.
r: Joshua 15:62; Song of Songs 1:14; Ezekiel 47:10; 2 Chronicles 20:2

a: the Ibex Rocks
p: The Hebrew names the cliffs after the ya'elim, the wild goats that still live at En-gedi.
b: The ya'el is the Nubian ibex, a wild goat with curved horns that leaps along the cliffs around En-gedi; Job 39:1 and Psalm 104:18 mention it. The name Jael, the woman who killed Sisera (Judges 4:17–22), means "ibex." Three thousand picked men against six hundred: Saul brings an army to catch an outlaw in country where an army is nearly useless.

a: Saul stepped inside to relieve himself
p: The Hebrew says Saul went in "to cover his feet," a polite way of saying he went to relieve himself.
b: The same phrase is used when Eglon's servants think their king is in his toilet room (Judges 3:24). A man squatting with his robe spread around him would "cover his feet." The Aramaic Targum explains it plainly as relieving himself. Some older readers took it to mean that Saul lay down to sleep, which would explain how David could cut his robe unnoticed, but most scholars prefer the first meaning. Either way the king is at his most helpless, in the dark, without guards.
orig: לְהָסֵךְ אֶת־רַגְלָיו (lehasekh et raglav), "to cover his feet"

a: Deep in the back of the cave sat David and his men
p: Two psalms are set "in the cave." Their prayers fit a man hiding from a king.
b: Psalm 57 is headed "when he ran away from Saul into the cave" (Psalm 57:0), and it prays, "Be gracious to me, God, be gracious to me, for my soul takes refuge in you. In the shadow of your wings I shelter until the disasters pass by" (Psalm 57:1). Psalm 142 is headed "A maskil of David, when he was in the cave. A prayer" (Psalm 142:0). It cries, "Look to my right side and see: there is nobody who knows me. Every way of escape has failed me; no one asks after my life," and then, "You are my place of shelter, my allotted share in the land of the living" (Psalm 142:4–5). Many scholars think the headings were added by later editors who read the psalms alongside Samuel; even so, they show how early readers heard these psalms.

a: The LORD said to you
p: No such promise is recorded. David's men may be twisting God's words, or quoting one we never hear.
b: Nowhere does the book record the LORD saying, "I will put your enemy in your hand." Some readers think the men are quoting a promise given through Gad or Samuel and not written down; Jonathan's words come close (20:15). Others think they are reading God's will from the circumstances: the enemy is here, so God must want him dead. Abishai will say the same thing in 26:8. David's answer is that an opportunity is not a command. A promise from God does not give him permission to grab what God has promised.

a: he sliced off the edge of the robe Saul had on
p: The hem of a robe stood for the person who wore it. To cut it was to cut into his status.
b: When Saul tore the edge of Samuel's robe, Samuel told him that the LORD had torn the kingdom from him that same day (15:27–28). Now David holds a piece of Saul's. In the ancient Near East the hem or fringe of a garment could stand for its owner: in letters from Mari (1700s BC) a prophet's hair and hem were sent to the king to vouch for him, and cutting a wife's hem could mean divorce. Ruth asks Boaz to spread his "wing" (the same word, kanaf) over her (Ruth 3:9). David's small cut is a large act, and his conscience knows it (24:5).

a: David's heart struck him
p: Hebrew has no word for "conscience"; it says David's heart struck him. The rabbis drew a lesson about clothing.
b: The idiom "his heart struck him" appears again when David counts his troops against God's will (2 Samuel 24:10). Both times David feels guilt before anyone accuses him. The Talmud says that because David showed disrespect for a garment here, garments would not keep him warm in his old age: "They piled clothes on him, but he could not get warm" (1 Kings 1:1; Berakhot 62b). The rabbis read the small act as serious because it was done to the LORD's anointed.
orig: וַיַּךְ לֵב־דָּוִד אֹתוֹ (vayyakh lev David oto), "David's heart struck him"

a: the LORD's anointed
p: David's reason for sparing Saul: the king is mashiach YHWH, "the LORD's anointed."
b: The word mashiach and its later history as "Messiah" are explained at 2:10 and 12:3. In these chapters the phrase becomes David's rule of conduct. He uses it of Saul seven times (twice in 24:6, then 24:10; 26:9, 11, 16, 23), always to explain why he will not strike. The office belongs to God, so ending it is God's business. The same reasoning makes David execute the Amalekite who claims to have killed Saul (2 Samuel 1:14–16).

a: David tore into his men with these words
p: The verb is a violent one: the word used for Samson tearing a lion apart.
b: The Hebrew shissa' means "tear apart." It is used when Samson tears a lion in two with his bare hands (Judges 14:6) and when a priest tears a bird open (Leviticus 1:17). Here it describes words, not hands. David's men are angry and armed; it takes force to stop them. The violence that might have fallen on Saul falls on David's own men as a rebuke.

a: 'Out of the wicked comes wickedness.'
p: This is the only proverb in the Old Testament labeled as an old saying of the ancients.
b: David quotes "the proverb of the ancients" (meshal haqqadmoni). His point is simple: evil people do evil things, and I have done none; if I were the plotter they say I am, you would be dead. Jesus makes a similar argument: "from their fruits you will know them" (Matthew 7:16–20; Luke 6:45). Ezekiel quotes another popular proverb only to reject it (Ezekiel 18:2). David's proverb also turns back on Saul, whose actions show what is in him.

a: A dead dog. One flea.
p: David calls himself worthless, using insults common in the ancient world.
b: A dog in Israel was a scavenger, not a pet, and a dead dog was the lowest thing imaginable. Mephibosheth calls himself "a dead dog" before David (2 Samuel 9:8), and Abishai calls Shimei one (2 Samuel 16:9). Letters from Canaan and Lachish use "your servant, a dog" as a humble form of address. David's "one flea" adds mockery: a king with three thousand men chasing a single flea. He uses the image again in 26:20.
orig: כֶּלֶב מֵת (kelev met), "dead dog"; פַּרְעֹשׁ אֶחָד (par'osh echad), "one flea"

a: Is this your voice, my son David?
p: Saul cannot see David clearly, so he asks about his voice. Blind Isaac once asked the same kind of question.
b: David is shouting from a distance, perhaps across a gorge, and Saul knows him by his voice. The question returns word for word in 26:17. Readers have recalled old Isaac, who could not see and judged his son by touch and voice (Genesis 27:22). There Jacob deceived his father; here David is the honest son and Saul the father who has been blind. Saul calls him "my son" for the first time since he became his son-in-law.

a: You are in the right, not I
p: Saul's confession uses the same words Judah spoke about Tamar.
b: "You are more righteous than I" in Hebrew is tsaddiq attah mimmeni. Judah said nearly the same about Tamar when she proved he had wronged her (Genesis 38:26). In both stories a man in power admits in public that the one he was about to destroy is in the right. Judah's confession led to a change of heart; Saul's does not last, and two chapters later he is hunting David again.

a: I know that you will certainly reign
p: Saul says out loud what Jonathan said he knew. His words sound like a blessing, and his deeds stay the same.
b: Jonathan told David that "Saul my father knows it too" (23:17). Now Saul says it himself. Readers have debated why he keeps hunting a man he knows God has chosen. Some see a man divided against himself, who knows the truth in calm moments and is driven by a troubling spirit in others (16:14; 18:10). Others see despair: Saul cannot accept a future without his house on the throne, so he asks David to swear to spare his family (24:21). The C lens reads such scenes as part of an "apology" for David, written to show that even Saul admitted David's right to rule.

a: you will not cut off my offspring after me
p: David swears to spare Saul's descendants. Second Samuel tells how he kept it, and how he did not quite.
b: David made a similar promise to Jonathan (20:14–17, 42). As king he looks for anyone left of Saul's house to show them kindness and brings Jonathan's lame son Mephibosheth to his table (2 Samuel 9:1–13). Yet when a famine is blamed on Saul's guilt, David hands seven of Saul's descendants to the Gibeonites to be executed, sparing Mephibosheth "because of the oath of the LORD" (2 Samuel 21:1–9). Readers differ on whether David kept the spirit of this oath. Ancient kings usually wiped out the old royal family (1 Kings 15:29; 2 Kings 10:11), which is why Saul asks.

a: Then Samuel died
p: The last judge and the first great prophet since Moses dies between the two stories of David sparing Saul.
b: Samuel's death is told in one verse, and told again in 28:3 to set up the scene at Endor. All Israel mourns, as it mourned for Moses (Deuteronomy 34:8). He is buried "at his house," which may mean on his family land; families often had tombs near home. A hilltop north of Jerusalem, Nebi Samwil, has been honored as his tomb since at least the Byzantine period, though the Bible places him in Ramah. Later Scripture remembers him with Moses as a great intercessor (Jeremiah 15:1; Psalm 99:6) and as the first of the prophets (Acts 3:24; Hebrews 11:32).
r: 28:3; 7:15–17; Deuteronomy 34:8; Jeremiah 15:1; Psalm 99:6; Acts 3:24; Hebrews 11:32; Sirach 46:13–20

a: A man in Maon had his work in Carmel
t: Maon, Carmel and the shearing feast
p: This Carmel is a village in Judah, not the famous mountain. Sheep-shearing was a time of feasting and generosity.
b: Maon (Khirbet Ma'in) and Carmel (Khirbet el-Kirmil) were neighboring villages about 8 miles south of Hebron, on the edge of the wilderness (Joshua 15:55). Saul set up a monument at this Carmel after his war with Amalek (15:12). Shearing time was a festival: Judah went up to his shearers at Timnah (Genesis 38:12), and Absalom invited all the princes to his (2 Samuel 13:23–28). A host was expected to share. That is why David's request is reasonable, and Nabal's refusal is an insult.

a: She was a woman of good sense and lovely to look at
p: The rabbis counted Abigail among Israel's seven prophetesses and its four most beautiful women.
b: The Talmud lists seven women as prophetesses: Sarah, Miriam, Deborah, Hannah, Abigail, Huldah and Esther (Megillah 14a). Abigail earns the title because she foretells David's lasting house (25:28–31). The same passage counts her with Sarah, Rahab and Esther as the four most beautiful women in the world (Megillah 15a). The rabbis also note her wit: in their retelling she persuades David that he cannot judge Nabal at night, when capital cases may not be tried. The narrator gives her two qualities, tovat sekhel, "good of understanding," and beauty, and puts the first one first.

a: To life!
p: The Hebrew greeting lechai is unclear. It may mean "to life," "to the living one" or, with one letter changed, "to my brother."
b: The word lechai appears only here. Most take it as a wish, "to life!", like the later Jewish toast l'chaim. Others read it "to him who lives," a polite way of addressing Nabal. A slight change gives le'achi, "to my brother," which some ancient translations seem to have read. Whatever the word, the greeting is warm and generous: peace three times over.

a: we have come on a good day
t: A fair request or protection money?
p: David asks for a share of the feast because his men guarded Nabal's flocks. Some modern historians call it a protection racket.
b: In the story's own terms, David's request is just: his men protected Nabal's shepherds from raiders (25:7, 15–16), and a feast day was a time for gifts (Nehemiah 8:10–12; Esther 9:19). Nabal's own servant confirms it. Some historians reading the story critically (the C lens), such as Baruch Halpern and Steven McKenzie, note that armed men who "protect" a rich farmer and then come for payment sound like a protection racket, and that David's response to a refusal is to plan a massacre. Readers in the H and L lenses answer that the narrator presents Nabal, not David, as the one in the wrong, and that the chapter itself shows David being stopped from evil.

a: These days there are plenty of slaves running off, every one from his master
p: Nabal calls David a runaway slave. In a way he is right: David did run from his master, Saul.
b: "Who is David?" is an insult: Nabal knows perfectly well who the son of Jesse is. Pharaoh asked the same scornful question about the LORD (Exodus 5:2). By calling David a runaway slave, Nabal sides with Saul. The irony is that the description fits: David has broken away from his lord. The law of Moses, in fact, told Israel not to hand a runaway slave back to his master (Deuteronomy 23:15–16).

a: he flew at them screaming
p: The verb comes from the word for a bird of prey. Nabal attacked David's men with words the way a hawk attacks.
b: The Hebrew vayya'at is related to 'ayit, "bird of prey." The same verb describes Saul's troops swooping on the spoil after battle (14:32) and Saul himself swooping on the plunder of Amalek (15:19). Nabal behaves like Saul: greedy, sudden, scornful. The young servant's choice of word shows how badly the visit went.

a: he is a worthless man
p: The servant calls his master a ben beliyya'al, "a son of worthlessness." Later writers made Belial a name for Satan.
b: On the word beliyya'al, "worthlessness," see 1:16 and 2:12. Here a servant uses it of his own master, and Abigail will say the same of her husband (25:25). Later the phrase returns for the troublemakers among David's own men who refuse to share the spoil (30:22). By the time of the Dead Sea Scrolls, Belial had become the name of the chief evil spirit, and Paul asks, "What agreement has Christ with Belial?" (2 Corinthians 6:15).

a: Abigail moved fast
p: Her gift is a feast for six hundred men, packed and on the road within the hour.
b: Two hundred loaves, two skins of wine, five dressed sheep, about a bushel and a half of roasted grain, a hundred clusters of raisins and two hundred cakes of pressed figs: it is the food Nabal refused, and more. Abigail does not stop to ask her husband. Ziba later meets David with a similar load when David flees from Absalom (2 Samuel 16:1), and Barzillai feeds David's army (2 Samuel 17:27–29). The word for "skins" of wine is nivlei, which sounds like Nabal: she brings the "nabals" of wine that will finish him (25:37).

a: a single male of Nabal's
p: The Hebrew is coarse: "anyone who pees against a wall." The KJV kept it; modern versions soften it.
b: David's oath literally says he will not leave "one who urinates against a wall," a soldier's crude way of saying "a single male." The same phrase is used in prophets' curses on royal houses (1 Kings 14:10; 16:11; 21:21; 2 Kings 9:8), and the KJV translated it word for word ("any that pisseth against the wall"). The Plain English gives the meaning, as most modern versions do, but the crudeness shows how angry David is. He repeats it in 25:34, after Abigail has calmed him.
orig: מַשְׁתִּין בְּקִיר (mashtin beqir), "one urinating against a wall"

a: Put the guilt on me, my lord, on me
p: Abigail begins by taking the blame herself, a move the wise woman of Tekoa will copy.
b: Abigail has done nothing wrong, but she takes responsibility for her house so that she can speak for it. Judah offered himself in Benjamin's place in the same spirit (Genesis 43:9; 44:32–34). The wise woman of Tekoa, sent by Joab to persuade David, opens with almost the same words (2 Samuel 14:9). Abigail's speech (25:24–31) is one of the longest speeches by a woman in the Bible, and one of the most skillful: humble in form, bold in content, and full of the promises God has made to David.

a: Nabal is his name, and shameful folly is his companion
p: In Hebrew a nabal is a fool in the moral sense: a man who lives as if there were no God.
b: Nabal is not a fool for lack of brains but for lack of conscience: "'There is no God,' the fool says to himself" (Psalm 14:1). Nevalah, "shameful folly," is the word for outrageous acts like the rape of Dinah (Genesis 34:7) or the crime at Gibeah (Judges 19:23). No parent would name a child that; some think the narrator gives him a nickname, or that the name meant something else, like "noble" (as in Arabic nabil), and Abigail twists it. Her wordplay continues in 25:37, where the wine (in nevel, a wineskin) goes out of him.

a: from taking your rescue into your own hand
p: Abigail's main argument: vengeance belongs to God, and a future king should not start with innocent blood.
b: The Hebrew says "from your hand saving you," that is, from getting justice for yourself by force. This is the lesson David has just shown in the cave (24:12, 15) and is about to forget. The law says vengeance belongs to God (Deuteronomy 32:35), and Paul quotes that verse: "Beloved, never take revenge yourselves, but make room for the anger" (Romans 12:19). Abigail speaks as if Nabal's punishment is already settled; ten days later God strikes him (25:38).

a: The LORD will certainly build my lord a house that stands firm
p: Abigail foretells David's dynasty in the same words God will use through Nathan.
b: "A firm house," bayit ne'eman, is a dynasty that lasts. God promised one to a faithful priest in place of Eli's (2:35); Nathan will promise one to David (2 Samuel 7:16); and Ahijah will offer one to Jeroboam if he obeys (1 Kings 11:38). Abigail says it first, before Nathan, which is why the rabbis counted her a prophetess. She also calls David the one who "fights the battles of the LORD," the words Saul used when he offered David his daughter (18:17).

a: the bundle of the living
t: "Bound up in the bundle of the living"
p: Abigail's image became the words carved on Jewish gravestones for centuries.
b: Tseror hachayyim is a pouch or bundle, such as a shepherd might carry. Otto Eissfeldt pointed to the ancient practice of keeping a bag of small stones to count a flock: each stone stood for one animal, and those in the bag were "accounted for." Abigail pictures God keeping David's life safe in his own pouch. Jewish tradition took the phrase as a picture of the soul safe with God after death. The letters tav, nun, tsade, bet, he, short for "May his (or her) soul be bound up in the bundle of life," are carved on Jewish tombstones, and the words are part of the memorial prayer El Malei Rachamim.
orig: צְרוֹר הַחַיִּים (tseror hachayyim), "bundle of the living"

a: fling out from the cup of a sling
p: Abigail's picture of God's justice uses David's own weapon.
b: David killed Goliath with a sling (17:49–50). Abigail turns the image around: God will keep David's life like a stone safe in a pouch, and throw his enemies away like a stone whirled out of a sling. Jeremiah uses the same picture for God throwing his people out of the land (Jeremiah 10:18). Abigail is reminding David, without saying so, of the giant he beat without a sword. He needs no sword against Nabal either.

a: He will appoint you ruler over Israel
p: Abigail uses nagid, the title Samuel used when he anointed Saul and when he announced David.
b: The meaning of nagid, a ruler designated by God, is explained at 9:16 and 13:14. What stands out here is the speaker. Samuel used the word for Saul (10:1) and for the unnamed man who would replace him (13:14). Now Abigail, a woman of Judah, applies it to David by name, before any prophet has done so in public. God will remind David that he took him from the pasture to be nagid over Israel (2 Samuel 7:8).

a: throwing a feast in his house fit for a king
p: Many readers see Nabal as a stand-in for Saul, set between the two chapters where David spares Saul.
b: Robert Gordon and Jon Levenson drew attention to the parallels. Nabal feasts "like a king." He returns David evil for good, as Saul does (24:17; 25:21). God strikes him dead, as David says God will strike Saul (25:38; 26:10). And David's "Blessed be the LORD" at Nabal's death (25:39) hints at what Saul's death will mean. Placed between chapters 24 and 26, the story shows what David might have done to Saul, and what God will do instead. Levenson also notes that Abigail's marriage gives David a foothold in the Calebite lands around Hebron, where he will first be crowned (2 Samuel 2:1–4).

a: His heart died in his chest, and he turned to stone
p: Nabal seems to suffer a stroke or heart attack. The Hebrew also plays on his name.
b: "His heart died within him" and "he became stone" suggest paralysis, perhaps a stroke, ten days before death (25:38). Hebrew writers did not separate body and feelings as we do; the shock and the illness are one event. There is also wordplay: "when the wine had gone out" of Nabal echoes nevel, "wineskin" (25:18). The fool (nabal) is emptied like a wineskin (nevel), and the heart that was "merry" (25:36) dies.
orig: וַיָּמָת לִבּוֹ בְּקִרְבּוֹ (vayyamot libbo beqirbo), "his heart died within him"

a: Then the LORD struck Nabal down, and he died
p: The narrator says plainly that the LORD struck Nabal. David will say the same may happen to Saul.
b: The verb nagaf, "strike," is used for God's plagues (Exodus 12:23) and for defeat in battle (4:2). David will tell Abishai that "the LORD will strike him" (26:10), using the same verb of Saul. Readers in the H lens see God's direct judgment. Others note that the narrator, who rarely says what God does, says it here, so that the lesson of the chapter cannot be missed: David did not need to act.

a: to wash the feet of my lord's servants
p: Abigail answers David's proposal with the humblest service of the ancient household.
b: Washing a guest's dusty feet was the work of the lowest slave (Genesis 18:4; Luke 7:44). Abigail, a wealthy widow, offers to do it for David's servants, not even for David. Christian readers have often recalled Jesus washing his disciples' feet, the master taking the slave's place (John 13:4–15), and 1 Timothy 5:10 lists washing the feet of God's people among a widow's good works. Abigail's words are courtesy, but they fit her whole character.

a: David had already taken Ahinoam from Jezreel
p: Saul's wife was also named Ahinoam. A few scholars think David took her; most think this is another woman.
b: This Jezreel is a town in the hills of Judah near Maon and Carmel (Joshua 15:55–56). Ahinoam will bear David's firstborn, Amnon (2 Samuel 3:2). The Hebrew "had taken" can mean before or around the time of Abigail. The case that she was Saul's wife. Jon Levenson and Baruch Halpern noted that only these two women bear the name in the Bible. God tells David, "I gave you your master's house and put your master's wives into your lap" (2 Samuel 12:8). Taking a ruler's women was a claim to his throne: Abner and Rizpah (2 Samuel 3:7), Absalom (2 Samuel 16:21–22), Adonijah's request for Abishag (1 Kings 2:22). And this verse sets David's taking Ahinoam beside Saul's taking Michal from him. The case against. Saul's Ahinoam was the mother of Jonathan, a grown commander years earlier (13:2; 14:50), yet David's Ahinoam bears his first son later still, at Hebron. She is "of Jezreel," a town of Judah, not "daughter of Ahimaaz." And "your master's wives" may be stock language for inheriting a royal house. Most commentators mention the theory and set it aside, or leave it open.
r: 14:50; 13:2; Joshua 15:56; 2 Samuel 3:2; 2 Samuel 3:7; 2 Samuel 12:8; 2 Samuel 16:21–22; 1 Kings 2:22

a: Saul, meanwhile, had handed his daughter Michal
p: Saul uses his daughter as a political tool. David will later take her back, and her second husband will weep.
b: Michal loved David and saved his life (18:20; 19:11–17). Giving her to another man cancels David's place in the royal family. When David later demands her back as a condition for peace, Paltiel (as 2 Samuel calls him) follows her, weeping, until Abner sends him home (2 Samuel 3:13–16). The law of Deuteronomy 24:1–4 forbade a man to take back a wife who had married another after a divorce; whether this was a divorce is not clear. Michal is never asked what she wants.

a: Men of Ziph came to Saul at Gibeah
p: Chapters 24 and 26 tell very similar stories. Scholars differ on whether they describe one event or two.
b: Both chapters have the Ziphites' report, three thousand picked men, Saul at David's mercy, David's men urging him to kill, David's refusal to touch "the LORD's anointed," a token taken, a speech from a distance, Saul calling "my son David" and admitting his wrong. Many critical scholars (the C lens) see two versions of one tradition, kept side by side. Traditional readers (H) see two events, and point to the differences: day and night, a cave and a camp, a robe and a spear and jug. Literary readers (L) see a deliberate pair: the second story raises the stakes, and between them stands Nabal (chapter 25).

a: Abner son of Ner, his army commander
p: Abner was Saul's cousin and general. After Saul's death he will make Saul's son king, and then change sides.
b: Abner son of Ner was Saul's cousin (14:50–51). He brought young David to Saul after Goliath's death (17:55–57). After Gilboa he will set up Saul's son Ish-bosheth as king (2 Samuel 2:8–9), fight David's men, then go over to David, and be murdered by Joab (2 Samuel 3:6–39). Here he is the professional soldier caught asleep. David's mockery (26:14–16) may also be aimed at the man who will be his greatest rival for Israel's loyalty.

a: Ahimelech the Hittite
p: David's band included foreigners like Ahimelech the Hittite, and kinsmen like Abishai, his sister's son.
b: "Hittites" in Canaan may have been descendants of the great Hittite empire's people, or a local group bearing the name (Genesis 23:3). Another Hittite, Uriah, will be among David's best soldiers (2 Samuel 11:3; 23:39). Abishai and his brothers Joab and Asahel are sons of Zeruiah, David's sister (1 Chronicles 2:16). Abishai is brave and quick to kill: he will offer to cut off Shimei's head (2 Samuel 16:9) and again later (2 Samuel 19:21). David's "What do I have to do with you, sons of Zeruiah?" shows how often he had to hold them back.
r: Genesis 23:3; 2 Samuel 11:3; 2 Samuel 16:9–10; 2 Samuel 19:21–22; 2 Samuel 23:18; 1 Chronicles 2:16

a: His spear was driven into the ground beside his head
p: The spear Saul threw at David marks the king's place. David takes it, and with it the sign of Saul's power.
b: Saul's spear goes with him everywhere: he throws it at David twice (18:10–11; 19:9–10) and at Jonathan once (20:33), and he holds it at court (22:6). Abishai wants to use it to pin Saul to the ground "just once" (26:8), as Saul had tried to pin David to the wall. Instead David carries it off and calls across to Saul to send someone for it (26:22). In ancient art a king's spear was a mark of royal power; here it is held out to be returned, a sign that David will not take the kingdom by force.

a: Who has ever stretched out his hand against the LORD's anointed and gone unpunished?
p: David's words were used to argue for the divine right of kings, and against it.
b: In the 1600s, defenders of the divine right of kings, such as James I of England, cited this verse with Psalm 105:15 (in the KJV, "Touch not mine anointed") to argue that a king may never be resisted. Their opponents, such as the Scottish minister Samuel Rutherford in Lex, Rex (1644), answered that David did resist Saul, with six hundred armed men, while refusing to kill him, and that a king who breaks God's law can be opposed. Today the verse is sometimes used to shield church leaders from criticism, though Psalm 105:15 speaks of the patriarchs, not of rulers. In context David's point is narrower: God, not David, will decide Saul's end (26:10).

a: the LORD will strike him, and no one else
p: David lists three ways God might end Saul's life. The third is the one that happens.
b: David sees three possibilities: a blow from God, like the one that killed Nabal (25:38, the same verb); a natural death; or death in battle. Saul will "go down to the battle" against the Philistines and die on Gilboa (31:1–6). David's restraint did not change the outcome; it changed who was responsible for it. Some readers see the shadow of all three: Saul dies in battle, by his own hand, and as the LORD's judgment (1 Chronicles 10:13–14).

a: the LORD's own deep sleep had dropped over them
t: A deep sleep from the LORD
p: The Hebrew tardemah is the deep sleep God sent on Adam and on Abram.
b: Tardemah is no ordinary sleep: "So the LORD God made a deep sleep fall on the man, and he slept" (Genesis 2:21), and "a deep sleep fell on Abram" (Genesis 15:12) before God made his covenant with him. Isaiah speaks of a "spirit of deep sleep" poured out by the LORD (Isaiah 29:10). By calling it the LORD's sleep, the narrator tells us that David's daring raid succeeded because God shut the camp's eyes. It is one of the few places in these chapters where God acts directly.

a: you men are as good as dead
p: The Hebrew calls Abner's men "sons of death," meaning they deserve to die.
b: "Son of" in Hebrew can mean "one who belongs to" or "one who deserves." Saul used the same phrase of David: "he is a son of death" (20:31), and David uses it in anger at the rich man in Nathan's parable (2 Samuel 12:5). Guards who let an enemy reach the king's head would be executed in any army. David's mocking speech turns Saul's sentence on David back on Saul's own guards.

a: let him breathe in the scent of an offering
t: If God has stirred Saul up
p: David allows that God may be behind Saul's hatred. If so, an offering may calm him.
b: The Hebrew says "let him smell an offering," as God "smelled the soothing smell" of Noah's sacrifice and was moved to mercy (Genesis 8:21). Elsewhere the Bible speaks of God stirring people up, as when an evil spirit from the LORD troubled Saul (16:14) or God moved David to count Israel (2 Samuel 24:1). David's reasoning is: if this comes from God, let Saul make an offering and seek peace; if it comes from slanderers, let them be cursed. The word minchah here means any gift or offering.
orig: יָרַח מִנְחָה (yarach minchah), "let him smell an offering"

a: 'Go, serve other gods.'
p: To be forced out of Israel's land felt like being forced away from Israel's God. The Talmud built a teaching on this verse.
b: Ancient peoples linked each god with his land. Naaman took two mule loads of Israel's soil home so he could worship the LORD in Syria (2 Kings 5:17), and the exiles asked how they could sing the LORD's song in a foreign land (Psalm 137:4). David means that by chasing him abroad, his enemies push him toward foreign gods. The Talmud quotes this verse to teach that "whoever lives outside the Land of Israel is like one who has no God" (Ketubot 110b). The irony is that David's next move (27:1) is to go to Philistia himself.

a: the way a man chases a partridge over the hills
p: The Hebrew name for the partridge is qore', "the caller." David has just been calling from the hilltop.
b: The bird named here is probably the sand partridge or chukar of the Judean hills. Hunters chased it on foot until it tired and could be struck with a stick or a throwing stone. Its Hebrew name, qore', means "caller," from its loud cry. David has just "called" (qara') to Abner from the top of the hill (26:14). He is the calling bird on the mountain, chased by the king of Israel. Jeremiah also uses the partridge in a proverb (Jeremiah 17:11).

a: I have played the fool
p: Saul admits what Samuel told him long before, using the same word.
b: When Saul offered the sacrifice without waiting for Samuel, the prophet told him, using the verb sakhal, that he had acted foolishly (13:13). Now Saul says it of himself: hiskalti. He also says "I have sinned," as he did when Samuel rejected him (15:24, 30). David will use the same words when he sins by counting the people (2 Samuel 24:10). The difference between the two kings is not that one sins and the other does not, but what each does next.

a: What you set out to do, you will do, and you will win out.
p: These are Saul's last words to David. The two never meet again.
b: Saul blesses David as a father blesses a son, and admits David will succeed, as he did in 24:20. Then David goes "on his road" and Saul "to his place," and their paths do not cross again. Saul's next appearance is at Endor, where he hears the end of his story from Samuel (28:17–19). Literary readers note how often Saul's words in these chapters are true while his actions deny them, a picture of a man who sees clearly and cannot change.

a: David said in his heart
p: For the first time David makes a big move without asking God or a prophet. He goes to Israel's enemies.
b: Gad had told David to go back to Judah (22:5), and David had complained that his enemies were driving him to serve other gods (26:19). Now, "in his heart," he decides to do just that. No ephod is consulted, and no prophet speaks. Some readers see a lapse of faith, the low point of David's wilderness years; others see wise realism, since Saul would never stop. The narrator does not judge, but the sixteen months that follow are full of lies and killing, and they end with Ziklag in ashes (30:1–6).

a: Achish son of Maoch, the king of Gath
p: This is probably the same king David fooled in 21:10–15. This time David comes with an army.
b: In chapter 21 David came alone and had to act mad to escape. Now he comes with six hundred men and their families, a force worth having. Achish, at war with Saul, welcomes a famous defector. A king named "Achish son of Maacah" still ruled Gath about forty years later (1 Kings 2:39); he may be the same man in old age or his grandson, since names often ran in royal families.

a: This is how Ziklag came to belong to the kings of Judah
p: Ziklag's location is still debated. The note "kings of Judah" shows the narrator writing after the kingdom split.
b: Ziklag was a town of the far south, listed for Judah and for Simeon (Joshua 15:31; 19:5). It has been placed at Tel Sera', Tel Halif and other mounds; since 2019 the excavators of Khirbet al-Ra'i, near Kiryat Gat, have argued that it is Ziklag, though others doubt it. The words "the kings of Judah, as it still does today" assume a time when Judah had its own line of kings, separate from Israel's, which began after Solomon (about 930 BC). The book was finished, or at least edited, after that. David's men gathered there (1 Chronicles 12:1–22).

a: a year and four months
p: The Hebrew says "days and four months." "Days" here means a full year.
b: Yamim, "days," sometimes means "a year" (Leviticus 25:29; Judges 17:10; 1:3). So David lived among the Philistines for a year and four months, ending with Saul's death. Achish's remark that David had been with him "days and years" (29:3) is an exaggeration of a host who has come to trust him.

a: David would strike the land and leave no man or woman living
p: David kills everyone in the towns he raids so no one can tell Achish the truth. Readers have judged this very differently.
b: The text gives David's motive plainly in 27:11: dead people tell no tales. Many modern readers, Jewish and Christian, call this a massacre, done to protect a lie, and note that the narrator does not use the language of God's ban (cherem) here. Others point out that the peoples raided include the Amalekites, whom Israel had been ordered to wipe out (15:3; Deuteronomy 25:17–19), and that David protects Judah's towns while pretending to raid them. Literary readers (L) see the narrator letting David's methods speak for themselves, and they note that when the Amalekites raid Ziklag, they kill no one (30:2).

a: The Kenite part of the Negev
p: David tells Achish he raids Judah and its allies, the Jerahmeelites and the Kenites. In fact he protects them.
b: The Negev is the dry south of Judah, around Beersheba and Arad. The Jerahmeelites were a clan of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:9, 25). The Kenites, the family of Moses' father-in-law, had settled among Judah near Arad (Judges 1:16; 4:11; 15:6). By naming them, David makes Achish believe he is attacking his own people. Later he sends gifts to these same towns (30:29), which shows where his loyalty really lay.

a: He has made himself stink to his own people
p: The Hebrew idiom for becoming hated is "to make oneself stink."
b: Hiv'ish means "to make foul-smelling." Jacob complained that Simeon and Levi had made him stink to the people of the land (Genesis 34:30), and Israel's foremen told Moses he had made them stink to Pharaoh (Exodus 5:21). Saul's victory once made Israel stink to the Philistines (13:4). Achish believes David has done this to himself among Israel, and so can never go back. He is wrong, and the reader knows it.
orig: הַבְאֵשׁ הִבְאִישׁ (hav'esh hiv'ish), "he has made himself stink"

a: the guard of my head
p: Achish makes David "keeper of my head." Heads run through David's story, from Goliath's to Saul's.
b: "Keeper of my head" means bodyguard, but the phrase carries a dark irony. David made his name by cutting off a Philistine's head (17:51, 54). The Philistine commanders will ask how better David could win back Saul's favor than "with the heads of these men" (29:4). And the Philistines will cut off Saul's head (31:9). David's own answer, "Now you will know what your servant will do," is deliberately vague. Achish hears loyalty; the reader hears a threat.

a: Saul had removed the ghosts of the dead and the spirits that know things from the land
t: Ghosts of the dead and spirits that know things
p: The Hebrew ov and yidde'oni name the spirits of the dead and those who call them up. Saul had obeyed the law against them.
b: The law says: "Do not turn to the ghosts of the dead or to the spirits that know things" (Leviticus 19:31; also Leviticus 20:6, 27; Deuteronomy 18:11). Ov can mean a ghost, the person who calls it up, or perhaps a ritual pit; Harry Hoffner linked it to a Hittite word for a pit used to reach the underworld. Yidde'oni comes from "know." The Septuagint translated ov as engastrimythos, "belly-talker," and the Mishnah says the ba'al ov made the dead seem to speak from his armpit (Sanhedrin 7:7). In an early, faithful act, Saul had removed them. Now, desperate, he seeks one out.
r: Leviticus 19:31; Leviticus 20:6; Leviticus 20:27; Deuteronomy 18:10–12; Isaiah 8:19; Isaiah 29:4; 2 Kings 21:6; 2 Kings 23:24

a: pitched camp at Shunem
p: The two armies face each other across the Jezreel Valley. Endor lies behind the Philistine lines.
b: Shunem (modern Sulam) sits on the slope of the Hill of Moreh, on the north side of the Jezreel Valley; Mount Gilboa is the ridge on the south side, about 5 miles away. Endor lies north of the Hill of Moreh, so to reach it Saul must slip around the Philistine camp by night. Gideon fought the Midianites on this same ground (Judges 7:1), and Psalm 83:10 remembers Israel's enemies "who perished at Endor." The Philistines had marched up the coast and through the valley; holding it cut Saul off from the northern tribes. The scene at Endor takes place after the Philistines have moved from Aphek (29:1) to Jezreel (29:11), so chapter 28 is told out of time order, just before the battle.

a: whether through dreams, through the Urim or through the prophets
p: Dreams, the sacred lot and prophets were the lawful ways to ask God. None of them answers Saul.
b: God spoke to prophets in dreams and visions (Numbers 12:6), gave decisions through the Urim (Numbers 27:21), and raised up prophets so that Israel would not need diviners (Deuteronomy 18:14–15). Saul tries all three. The Urim may have been with another priest, since Abiathar had taken the ephod to David (23:6). Chronicles gives a sharper verdict: Saul died because he consulted a medium and "did not ask the LORD" (1 Chronicles 10:13–14). The rabbis reconciled the two by saying he did not seek God with his whole heart, or did not seek long enough. God had stopped answering Saul once before (14:37).

a: a woman for me who has a ghost at her call
p: The famous "witch of Endor" is never called a witch. The Hebrew calls her a ba'alat ov, "mistress of a ghost."
b: English Bibles since the KJV have often headed this chapter "the witch of Endor," but the text never uses the Hebrew word for a sorceress (mekhashefah, Exodus 22:18). She is a ba'alat ov, "owner" or "mistress" of a ghost: someone believed to control a spirit of the dead and make it speak. The difference matters: the story is not about spells or harm done to others but about necromancy, asking the dead for knowledge. She is also the only person in the chapter who shows kindness (28:21–25).
orig: אֵשֶׁת בַּעֲלַת־אוֹב (eshet ba'alat ov), "a woman, mistress of a ghost"

a: Saul made himself unrecognizable by putting on different clothes
p: Saul hides his royal clothes. Kings in disguise in the Bible usually meet bad news, and one of them dies in battle soon after.
b: Jeroboam's wife disguised herself to ask a prophet about her sick son and heard he would die (1 Kings 14:2–17). Ahab disguised himself for battle and was killed anyway (1 Kings 22:30–37), and so was Josiah (2 Chronicles 35:22). Clothing marks every turn of Saul's fall: he tore Samuel's robe (15:27), Jonathan gave his robe to David (18:4), David cut Saul's robe (24:4). Now the king takes off what makes him king. A midrash says that by "other clothes" the text means he had become another man, humbled (Leviticus Rabbah 26:7).

a: Use the ghost to read the future for me
p: Saul asks her to qesem, to practice divination. Samuel once compared rebellion to exactly this sin.
b: Qasam is the general word for reading omens and seeking hidden knowledge: Balaam's fee was for it (Numbers 22:7), and the law bans it (Deuteronomy 18:10). When Saul disobeyed at Amalek, Samuel told him that rebellion was like the sin of divination (15:23). Now Saul commits the sin itself, to reach the prophet who said it.
orig: קָסֳמִי־נָא לִי בָּאוֹב (qosomi-na li ba'ov), "divine for me by the ghost"

a: By the life of the LORD
t: An oath by the LORD for a medium
p: Saul swears by the LORD that the woman will not be punished for breaking the LORD's law.
b: The irony is heavy. Saul invokes the LORD to protect a practice the LORD forbids, and he does it as the king who had enforced that law. His oaths have gone wrong before: he swore that whoever ate before evening would die and nearly killed Jonathan (14:24, 39, 44); he swore not to kill David and broke it (19:6). Literary readers see the oath as the last sign of a king whose religion has become a tool.

a: The woman saw Samuel, and she let out a loud shriek
p: The woman screams the moment she sees Samuel. Each reading of the chapter explains the scream differently.
b: Readers who take the appearance as real point out that the text says plainly "the woman saw Samuel," and suggest she screamed because something happened that her art had never done: God himself sent Samuel. A midrash says she knew Saul because Samuel rose upright, while the dead raised for ordinary people came up upside down (Leviticus Rabbah 26:7). Those who think a demon appeared say the spirit revealed Saul's identity to win her trust. Those who think the scene was a fraud say the scream was theater: she had guessed who the tall stranger was, and the shriek let her accuse him first. See the chapter page for the three views at full length.

a: I see a divine being
p: The woman uses elohim, the word for God or gods, with a plural verb. The dead could be called elohim.
b: Literally she says, "I see elohim coming up out of the earth," and "coming up" is plural. Elohim can mean God, gods or divine beings; here it seems to mean a spirit of the dead, as in Isaiah 8:19, where people consult the dead as their "gods." Texts from Ugarit also call the dead gods. The Talmud took the plural literally: two figures came up, Samuel and Moses, because Samuel feared he was being summoned to judgment and brought Moses as a witness (Hagigah 4b). Saul then asks about one figure only.
orig: אֱלֹהִים רָאִיתִי עֹלִים (elohim ra'iti olim), "elohim I see, coming up" (plural)

a: he has a robe wrapped around him
p: Saul knows Samuel by his robe, the garment that marked Samuel from childhood to the day Saul tore it.
b: The me'il, a long outer robe, follows Samuel through the book. His mother made him a little one every year (2:19). When Samuel turned to leave Saul after Amalek, Saul grabbed its hem and tore it, and Samuel declared the kingdom torn away (15:27–28). David later cut the edge of Saul's own robe (24:4). Now the robe is all Saul needs to recognize Samuel, and he bows to the ground before it. Robert Polzin and Robert Alter both trace this chain of robes as a sign of the kingdom passing from Saul to David.

a: Why did you stir me up and bring me up here?
p: Samuel complains that Saul has "disturbed" him, the same verb used in ancient curses on grave robbers.
b: The verb ragaz means to shake or disturb. Phoenician kings of Sidon, about 500 BC, carved warnings on their coffins: do not open me and do not disturb me (the Tabnit and Eshmunazar inscriptions use the same root). Isaiah pictures Sheol "stirred up" to meet the king of Babylon (Isaiah 14:9). The dead in Israelite belief were at rest, and calling them up was a violation. The rabbis taught that a righteous man's soul could be raised in the first year after death, while the body was still in the grave (Shabbat 152b–153a), which fits Samuel's recent death.

a: So I called for you, to let me know what I should do
p: Jews and Christians have read the figure at Endor as the real Samuel, as a demon, or as a fraud. Each view has strong arguments.
b: Real Samuel: the narrator calls the figure Samuel five times, and his message comes true. Sirach says Samuel "prophesied after his death" (Sirach 46:20); Josephus, the Talmud, Justin Martyr, Origen and many modern evangelicals agree, often adding that God sent Samuel. A demon: Tertullian, Eustathius of Antioch, Gregory of Nyssa, Luther and Calvin held that God's prophet could not be summoned by a forbidden art, so an evil spirit took Samuel's form (2 Corinthians 11:14). Fraud: the Gaon Samuel ben Hofni (died 1013) and Reginald Scot (1584) said the woman tricked Saul; only she sees the figure, and "belly-talker" suggests ventriloquism. The chapter page sets out each view fully.

a: He has ripped the kingdom from your hand and handed it to your neighbor, to David
p: Samuel repeats almost word for word what he told Saul after the war with Amalek, and this time names the neighbor.
b: After Saul spared Agag, Samuel told him that the LORD had torn the kingdom from him and given it to a neighbor better than he (15:28). The figure at Endor says the same thing, adding the name: David. The repetition is one reason many readers believe it is truly Samuel, since the message matches his earlier word exactly. Those who hold the demon view answer that a lying spirit could quote a true prophecy to drive Saul to despair.

a: you did not pour out the heat of his anger on Amalek
p: Saul's failure with Amalek is named as the reason for his fall. Amalek will appear twice more before his story ends.
b: The LORD had sworn war on Amalek forever (Exodus 17:14–16; Deuteronomy 25:17–19), and Saul's failure to carry out the ban cost him the throne (15:1–35). Two chapters later the Amalekites burn Ziklag and carry off David's family (30:1–2), and David does what Saul did not. Then an Amalekite will come to David claiming to have finished Saul off (2 Samuel 1:1–16). The narrator lets Amalek frame Saul's end.

a: Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me
p: Saul will join Samuel among the dead. Does "with me" say anything about Saul's eternal fate?
b: Most readers take "with me" to mean in Sheol, the realm where all the dead go, good and bad alike (Ecclesiastes 9:10), not in the same reward. The Talmud read it more kindly: "with me" means "in my company," so Saul's death atoned for his sins and he would share Samuel's place (Berakhot 12b). Some Christian readers have compared Jesus' words to the thief (Luke 23:43). Others take the verse as a sentence of death and nothing more. "Tomorrow" may be meant literally, or loosely as "soon"; the battle comes in chapter 31.

a: his whole height stretched out on the ground
p: Saul was a head taller than everyone. Now his whole height lies on the ground.
b: When Saul was chosen he stood taller than anyone in Israel (9:2; 10:23), and his height impressed Israel, though God would later tell Samuel not to judge by height (16:7). The Hebrew says he fell "the fullness of his stature" to the ground. It is a picture of the whole reign: the man the people chose for his size, flat in a medium's house, before the battle has begun.

a: baked flat bread with no yeast
p: The woman serves the condemned king a meal fit for an honored guest. Josephus praised her generosity.
b: She kills her fattened calf and bakes bread in haste, as Abraham did for his three visitors (Genesis 18:6–8). Josephus closed his retelling with a long praise of her: she had nothing, yet gave her one calf to a man she would never see again, who had made her trade a crime (Antiquities 6.340–342). Christian readers have sometimes seen in it a last supper before death. The meal also gives Saul strength to go to the battle where he will die. Unleavened bread, made quickly, recalls the night of the Passover (Exodus 12:39).

a: Then they rose and walked away into that night
p: The chapter that began at night ends at night. It is Saul's last night alive.
b: Saul came "by night" (28:8) and leaves "that night" (28:25). In the next morning's battle he dies. Readers have compared Judas, who went out from the Last Supper "and it was night" (John 13:30). The narrator gives no last words and no prayer. Saul simply goes.

a: The Philistines brought all their armies together at Aphek
p: The Philistines gathered at Aphek, as they did before the battle where they took the ark.
b: Aphek (Tel Afek, at the springs of the Yarkon River near modern Rosh HaAyin) guarded the coastal road where it squeezed between the hills and the marshes. The Philistines mustered there before the battle that cost Israel the ark (4:1). From Aphek they marched north to the Jezreel Valley (29:11). So the scene at Endor, when the Philistines are already at Shunem (28:4), takes place after chapter 29 in time, at about the time of chapter 30.

a: What are these Hebrews?
p: In 1 Samuel, foreigners call Israelites "Hebrews." Israelites rarely call themselves that.
