b: On who used the word "Hebrews" and its possible link with the 'apiru, see 4:6 and 14:21. Here the word carries its sharpest edge. The Philistine commanders remember that "Hebrews" on their own side changed sides in the middle of a battle (14:21). That is exactly what they fear David will do.

a: He could turn into our adversary
p: The Hebrew word for "adversary" here is satan. It is an ordinary word before it becomes a name.
b: The commanders fear David will become lesatan, "an adversary," in the battle. The same word describes the angel who blocked Balaam's road (Numbers 22:22), David's own nephews (2 Samuel 19:22), and the enemies God raised against Solomon (1 Kings 11:14). Only later does "the satan" become the accuser in heaven (Job 1:6; Zechariah 3:1), and later still a personal name. The fear is reasonable: some Hebrews had switched sides once before (14:21).
r: 14:21; Numbers 22:22; 2 Samuel 19:22; 1 Kings 5:4; 1 Kings 11:14; Job 1:6; Zechariah 3:1

a: By the life of the LORD
t: A Philistine swears by the LORD
p: Achish swears by Israel's God. It may be courtesy to David, or the narrator's own wording.
b: It is unusual for a foreigner to swear by the LORD. Some think Achish is being polite, swearing by his guest's God, as Abimelech of Gerar spoke of the LORD with Isaac (Genesis 26:28) and Hiram of Tyre praised the LORD for Solomon (1 Kings 5:7). Others think the narrator has put Achish's oath into Israelite form. Either way, the pagan king's honesty and warmth stand out against Saul, who swore by the same God and broke his word.

a: that I may not go and fight the enemies of my lord the king
p: David protests that he wants to fight "the enemies of my lord the king." He does not say which king.
b: Achish hears "my lord the king" as himself, and the enemies as Israel. But David has called Saul "my lord the king" twice (24:8; 26:17). Readers have long asked what David would have done in the battle: fought his own people, deserted to Saul, or turned on the Philistines as the commanders feared. The narrator never tells us, and Robert Alter calls the phrase a masterpiece of ambiguity. The commanders' refusal spares David from having to choose.

a: as good as an angel of God
p: Others will say the same thing to flatter David, when he is king.
b: The woman of Tekoa tells David he is "like the angel of God," able to tell good from evil (2 Samuel 14:17, 20), and Mephibosheth says it again (2 Samuel 19:27). Paul says the Galatians received him "as an angel of God" (Galatians 4:14). From Achish the words are sincere: he has been completely deceived (27:12).

a: The Philistines went on up to Jezreel
p: David is spared from fighting Saul. The timing also lets him reach Ziklag in time to rescue his family.
b: If David had marched to Gilboa, he would have shared in Saul's death or betrayed his hosts. Either would have ruined his claim to Israel's throne. The Philistine commanders' distrust sends him home. Readers in the H lens see God's care in it; the narrator does not say so, but the pattern of narrow escapes (23:26–28) suggests it. Had he stayed even a few days longer, the Amalekites' trail at Ziklag would have gone cold (30:1–8).

a: It took David and his men until the third day to reach Ziklag
p: From Aphek to Ziklag is roughly 50 miles, a hard march of three days.
b: While David marched north with the Philistines, the town he left unguarded was raided. The Amalekites struck the whole Negev, not only Ziklag (30:14). Raids like this were common in the dry south, where nomads moved fast on camels. The timing is grimly ironic: David has spent sixteen months raiding the Amalekites (27:8), and they strike back the moment he is away.

a: the Amalekites had swept down
p: Saul had "destroyed" the Amalekites in chapter 15. Here they are, raiding in force.
b: Chapter 15 says Saul devoted all the Amalekite people to destruction (15:8, 20), yet Amalekites raid in chapters 27 and 30, four hundred escape (30:17), and they are still around in Hezekiah's day (1 Chronicles 4:42–43). Traditional readers explain that Saul struck one region, "from Havilah to Shur" (15:7), while other Amalekite clans lived elsewhere. Critical scholars see separate traditions. Both note that the narrator lets the survivors of Saul's half-obedience become a scourge.

a: They put no one to death
p: The Amalekites take everyone alive. David, raiding them, had left no one alive.
b: The contrast with 27:9 and 27:11 is sharp: David killed every man and woman in the towns he raided, but the Amalekites keep their captives alive, probably to sell as slaves. Some readers see the narrator's quiet judgment on David's methods. Others note that it is the Amalekites' greed, not mercy, that saves David's family, and that God uses it.

a: because the troops were saying he should be stoned
p: In grief, David's men turn on him, as Israel once turned on Moses.
b: Moses cried to the LORD at Rephidim that the people were almost ready to stone him (Exodus 17:4), and at Kadesh the whole community spoke of stoning Joshua and Caleb (Numbers 14:10). David's men have lost everything because he took them on the Philistine march. Their anger is the price of his sixteen months in Philistia. At this point he has no friend, no town, no family, and no army he can trust.

a: But David made himself strong in the LORD his God
p: Saul, in his crisis, went to a medium. David, in his, turns to the LORD and asks through the ephod.
b: The two chapters are set side by side on purpose. Both kings face disaster. Saul asks God and hears nothing, then breaks the law to reach Samuel (28:6–8). David strengthens himself in the LORD, calls for the ephod, asks, and is answered (30:7–8). Jonathan had once strengthened David's hand in God (23:16); now David does it alone. Many readers, Jewish and Christian, treat this verse as the spiritual turning point of David's wilderness years: after his own scheming in Philistia, he goes back to asking.

a: the Besor wadi
p: The Besor is the great dry riverbed of the northwestern Negev, flowing toward the sea south of Gaza.
b: A nachal, or wadi, is a streambed that runs only after rains. The Besor (Wadi Ghazzeh) drains much of the northwestern Negev; its banks can be steep and its bed deep sand. Men who had already marched three days from Aphek, and found their homes burned, could go no farther. Leaving the weak behind with the baggage would become the basis of David's rule in 30:24–25.

a: his spirit came back into him
p: The Hebrew pictures life or strength as "spirit" (ruach) coming back. Samson revived the same way.
b: After three days without food or water, the Egyptian slave is near death. The phrase "his spirit returned to him" is used of Samson after God opened a spring for him (Judges 15:19). Ruach is breath, wind and spirit at once. A man left to die by his master becomes the key to David's victory, which readers have often taken as a lesson about the value of the least person.
orig: וַתָּשָׁב רוּחוֹ אֵלָיו (vattashov rucho elav), "his spirit returned to him"

a: Three days ago I fell sick, and my master left me lying
p: The Amalekite who left a sick slave in the desert lost everything because of it.
b: The law of Moses protected runaway slaves and warned Israel not to mistreat the helpless (Deuteronomy 23:15–16; Exodus 22:21–24). The Amalekite treats his slave as worthless; David's men give him bread, water, figs and raisins before asking a single question. The Egyptian then guides them to the camp. The rabbis and many Christian preachers have drawn the moral that kindness to the least can turn the course of events. The slave's request for an oath not to be returned to his master (30:15) shows what he expected from masters.

a: the Kerethite Negev
p: The Kerethites were probably Cretans, a people linked with the Philistines. Some later served as David's bodyguard.
b: Ezekiel and Zephaniah pair the Kerethites with the Philistines (Ezekiel 25:16; Zephaniah 2:5), and Amos says the Philistines came from Caphtor (Amos 9:7), usually identified with Crete. When David is king, "the Kerethites and the Pelethites" form his personal guard under Benaiah (2 Samuel 8:18; 15:18; 20:23). David's long stay among the Philistines may be how he recruited them.

a: four hundred young men who climbed onto camels
p: The Amalekites raid on camels, which outrun men on foot. Archaeology dates the domestic camel in this region to about this time.
b: Desert raiders on camels appear first in the time of Gideon (Judges 6:5; 7:12). Bones from copper-mining camps in the Aravah show domestic camels arriving in the southern Levant around the late 900s BC (Sapir-Hen and Ben-Yosef, 2013), close to David's time; camels in the stories of the patriarchs are more debated. Four hundred escape on camels, the same number of men David brought (30:10). Without camels, David cannot chase them.

a: This is David's spoil!
p: The Hebrew of this verse is unclear. It seems to set apart some of the flocks as David's own share.
b: Literally it reads: "David took all the flocks and the herds; they drove before that livestock, and they said, 'This is David's spoil.'" Who drove what before what is not clear. Most take it that the animals taken from the Amalekites' own herds, beyond what had been stolen from Ziklag, were driven at the front and declared David's. That would explain how David later had gifts to send to Judah's elders (30:26). Some ancient translations smooth the verse in different ways.
orig: וַיֹּאמְרוּ זֶה שְׁלַל דָּוִד (vayyomeru zeh shelal David)

a: every nasty, worthless man
p: The same "sons of Belial" phrase used of Nabal describes the men who want to cheat the weary.
b: The Hebrew calls them men of evil and beliyya'al, the word used of Nabal (25:17, 25). Not every man who followed David was a hero; some were the debtors and the bitter of 22:2. David calls them "brothers" anyway (30:23) and overrules them gently.

a: As the portion is for the one who goes down into the fight, so the portion will be for the one who stays by the gear
p: David's rule that those who guard the supplies share equally with the fighters became law in Israel.
b: Moses had divided the spoil from Midian half to the soldiers and half to the community (Numbers 31:27), and Joshua told the eastern tribes to share their spoil with their brothers (Joshua 22:8). David's rule is simpler: everyone who served shares alike, whether at the front or with the baggage. The reason he gives is theological: the spoil is what "the LORD has given us" (30:23), so no one earned it. Christian preachers have applied it to unseen work in the church; it also echoes the parable of the workers paid the same wage (Matthew 20:1–16).

a: a rule and a ruling for Israel
p: The Hebrew chok u-mishpat is the language of the law of Moses. David makes law before he is king.
b: Chok and mishpat, "rule" and "ruling," are the paired words Deuteronomy uses for God's laws (Deuteronomy 4:1), and Joshua made "a rule and a ruling" at Shechem (Joshua 24:25). The phrase "to this day" shows that David's rule was still observed when the story was written. An outlaw in exile is already acting like the lawgiver he will become.
orig: לְחֹק וּלְמִשְׁפָּט (lechoq ulemishpat), "for a rule and a ruling"

a: Here is a blessing for you, out of the spoil taken from the enemies of the LORD
p: David shares his spoil with the elders of Judah. It is generosity, and it is politics.
b: The towns in 30:27–31 are the places where David and his men had moved about, and they are the elders who will soon make him king at Hebron (2 Samuel 2:1–4). Calling the gift a "blessing" (as Abigail called hers, 25:27) and the Amalekites "the enemies of the LORD" presents David as Judah's protector. Some historians read it as buying support. Others see a leader paying back those who sheltered him. The two readings are not exclusive.

a: to the people in Hebron
p: The list runs through the hill country and the Negev of Judah and ends at Hebron, David's first capital.
b: Several towns can be located: Jattir (Khirbet Attir), Eshtemoa (es-Samu'), Aroer in the Negev, Hormah near Arad, and Hebron. "Bethel" here is probably the southern town also called Bethuel (Joshua 19:4; 1 Chronicles 4:30), not the famous Bethel in the north. "Ramoth of the Negev" may be the place called Ramah of the Negev in Joshua 19:8. Racal and Athach are otherwise unknown. Hebron comes last, the place where David will reign seven and a half years (2 Samuel 2:11).
r: Joshua 15:48–54; Joshua 19:4; Joshua 19:8; Joshua 21:13–14; 2 Samuel 2:1–4; 2 Samuel 2:11

a: their dead lay fallen on Mount Gilboa
p: Saul's last battle is told twice in the Bible, here and in 1 Chronicles 10, and lamented by David.
b: First Chronicles 10:1–12 copies this chapter almost word for word, then adds its own verdict on why Saul died (1 Chronicles 10:13–14). David's lament for Saul and Jonathan curses the mountain: "You mountains in Gilboa, / may no dew and no rain come down on you" (2 Samuel 1:21). Mount Gilboa is a ridge on the southeastern edge of the Jezreel Valley; the Israelites retreated up its slopes from the plain, where the Philistine chariots and archers had the advantage.

a: They cut down Saul's sons Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchishua
p: Three sons die with Saul. A fourth, Ish-bosheth, survives to become king for a short time.
b: An earlier list names Saul's sons as Jonathan, Ishvi and Malchishua (14:49); Chronicles names four: Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab and Eshbaal (1 Chronicles 8:33). Eshbaal, called Ish-bosheth in 2 Samuel, was not at Gilboa and is made king by Abner (2 Samuel 2:8–10). Jonathan, who had promised to stand at David's side (23:17), dies beside his father instead. David's lament says the two were "not parted" in life or death (2 Samuel 1:23).

a: he was in great anguish from the archers
p: The Hebrew verb can mean "writhe in pain" or "tremble with fear." The Greek says he was wounded.
b: Vayyachel comes from chil, used for the pains of a woman giving birth and for shaking with fear. The Greek says Saul was wounded in the abdomen, and the KJV follows it with "sore wounded." First Chronicles 10:3 repeats the same ambiguous Hebrew verb; only some English versions render it "wounded" there. Other readers, such as Robert Alter, take it as fear: Saul trembles before the archers and asks to be killed before they reach him. The Plain English uses "anguish," which keeps both.

a: these uncircumcised men will come and stab me and have their cruel fun with me
p: Saul fears what the Philistines did to Samson: capture, torture and public mockery.
b: "Uncircumcised" is Israel's word of contempt for the Philistines (14:6; 17:26, 36; Judges 14:3). The verb hit'allel, "make sport of," is used for the men of Gibeah abusing the Levite's concubine (Judges 19:25) and for God's dealings with Egypt (Exodus 10:2). Saul remembers Samson, blinded and made to perform for a Philistine crowd (Judges 16:21–25). Abimelech, dying, asked his armor-bearer to kill him so no one could say a woman had done it (Judges 9:54).

a: So Saul took hold of the sword and fell on it
t: Saul's death and the question of suicide
p: Saul takes his own life. Jews and Christians have judged his act in very different ways.
b: The narrator gives no verdict. Josephus praised Saul as a hero who chose death knowing it was coming (Antiquities 6.344–350). The rabbis, who generally forbade suicide, read Genesis 9:5 to allow an exception for someone like Saul, facing torture and the shaming of Israel (Genesis Rabbah 34:13). Augustine argued that suicide is never right, while not dealing with Saul at length (City of God 1.17–27). Chronicles reads his death as God's judgment (1 Chronicles 10:13–14). Second Samuel adds an Amalekite's claim that he finished Saul off at the king's request (2 Samuel 1:6–10), probably a lie to win David's favor. See the topic page for the Bible's other cases. The topic page also gathers the people in the Bible who wished to die and were met with care, and how Jews and Christians counsel today.
r: Genesis 9:5; Judges 9:54; 2 Samuel 1:6–10; 2 Samuel 17:23; 1 Kings 16:18; Matthew 27:5; 1 Chronicles 10:13–14

a: all his men
p: Chronicles says his whole house died with him. Samuel says "all his men." Neither means every last one.
b: First Chronicles 10:6 reads "So Saul and his three sons died, and his whole house died with them," which goes beyond Samuel, since Ish-bosheth and other descendants survived (2 Samuel 2:8; 21:8). Chronicles seems to mean that Saul's dynasty ended that day; Samuel's "all his men" probably means his personal guard. Either way, the day ended Saul's kingdom.

a: They hacked off his head
p: David cut off Goliath's head and carried it home. Now the Philistines do the same to Saul.
b: After killing Goliath, David cut off his head and brought it to Jerusalem (17:51, 54). Here the Philistines return the insult. First Chronicles 10:10 adds that they fastened Saul's head in the temple of Dagon, the god whose statue once fell headless before the ark (5:4). Displaying an enemy king's head and armor was common in the ancient world; Assyrian reliefs show it.

a: to bring the good news to their idols' temples
p: The Hebrew verb is basar, "bring good news," the word behind the Greek for "gospel."
b: Basar means to announce good news, usually of victory (2 Samuel 18:19–20). Isaiah uses it of the messenger who announces God's reign (Isaiah 52:7), and the Septuagint translates it with euangelizomai, from which comes "evangelize." Here the good news is announced to idols. David's lament begs that it not be told in Gath or proclaimed in the streets of Ashkelon (2 Samuel 1:20).
r: 2 Samuel 1:20; 2 Samuel 4:10; 2 Samuel 18:19–20; Isaiah 52:7; Isaiah 40:9; Luke 2:10

a: in the house of the Ashtaroth goddesses
p: Saul's armor went to a goddess's temple; his body was hung on the walls of Beth-shan, a fortress city in the Jordan Valley.
b: Ashtaroth is the plural of Ashtoreth (Astarte), a Canaanite goddess of love and war (Judges 2:13; 10:6; 7:3). Beth-shan (Tel Beth-Shean) guarded the eastern end of the Jezreel Valley; it had been an Egyptian garrison town, and excavators found a series of temples there. Alan Rowe, who dug in the 1920s, identified two Iron Age temples as the temple of Ashtaroth and the temple of Dagon mentioned in 1 Chronicles 10:10. Later archaeologists, including Amihai Mazar, have questioned that identification and the dating.

a: his corpse they fastened to the wall of Beth-shan
p: Israel's law said a hanged body must not stay up overnight. Saul's hangs on an enemy wall.
b: The law said "his body must not stay on the tree overnight" (Deuteronomy 21:23), and Joshua followed it with the kings he executed (Joshua 8:29; 10:26–27). To leave a body exposed was the worst disgrace, denying it burial. The verb taqa' means to drive in or fasten, as with a tent peg; the text does not say whether the bodies were nailed, tied or hung on hooks. Years later David brings the bones of Saul and Jonathan from Jabesh and buries them in the family tomb (2 Samuel 21:12–14).

a: Those living in Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul
p: Saul's first act as king was to rescue Jabesh-gilead. Its men repay him with his burial.
b: When Nahash the Ammonite threatened to gouge out the right eye of every man in Jabesh, Saul rallied Israel and saved the town (11:1–11). Jabesh also had old blood ties to Benjamin, Saul's tribe (Judges 21:8–14). Now its men walk all night, about 10 miles, to take the bodies down. David will bless them for their loyalty (2 Samuel 2:4–7). Saul's reign ends as it began, with the men of Jabesh.

a: Then they came to Jabesh and burned them there
p: Israel buried its dead and rarely burned them. Readers have offered several reasons for this burning.
b: Burning a body was usually a punishment (Leviticus 20:14; Joshua 7:25; Amos 2:1). Some think the men of Jabesh burned the bodies because they were mutilated and decaying, or to keep them from being taken again. Others think only the flesh was burned and the bones kept, which matches 31:13. Radak and other Jewish commentators took it as a burning of spices in their honor, as was done for kings (Jeremiah 34:5; 2 Chronicles 16:14). First Chronicles 10:12 leaves the burning out.

a: buried them beneath the tamarisk in Jabesh
p: Saul once held court under a tamarisk. Now his bones lie under one, mourned for seven days.
b: Saul sat under the tamarisk at Gibeah, spear in hand, when he ordered the priests killed (22:6). His bones rest under a tamarisk at Jabesh (1 Chronicles 10:12 says an oak or terebinth). Seven days of fasting was a full mourning, like Joseph's for Jacob (Genesis 50:10). Israel's first king, flawed and tragic, is honored at the end by the town he saved. David's lament follows in 2 Samuel 1.
